documentNotes.title: Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
**This question paper must not be photographed or taken out of the exam room**

**Time**: 3 hours ($\sim 65$ minutes for Q1, $\sim 70$ minutes for Q2 and $\sim 45$ minutes for Q3).

**Questions**: All three questions should be attempted. Each question contains independent parts so that later parts can be attempted even if earlier parts are incomplete.

**Solutions**: Answers and calculations are to be written on loose paper. **YOU WILL NEED GRAPH PAPER**. Students should ensure their **name** and **school** is clearly written on the **first** answer sheet and that **all** pages are numbered. **EACH QUESTION ANSWERED must be started on a new page.** A standard formula booklet with standard physical constants may be used if desired.

**Instructions**: To accommodate students sitting the paper at different times, please **do not discuss** any aspect of the paper on the internet until 8 am Saturday 11th February.

**Clarity**: Solutions must be written legibly, in black pen, and working down the page. Scribble will not be marked and overall clarity is an important aspect of this exam.

**Eligibility**: The International Olympiad will be held in August 2023; all sixth form students are eligible to participate.

**Calculators**: Any standard calculator may be used, but calculators cannot be programmable and must not have symbolic algebra capability.

**Training Dates and the IOAA** (Chorzów, Poland, 10th - 20th August 2023)

*The team will be selected from students taking this paper. The best students that are eligible to represent the UK at the IOAA will be invited to attend the* **Training Camp** *to be held in Oxford from* **Saturday 1st to Wednesday 5th April 2023**. *Astronomy material will be covered; problem solving skills and observational skills (telescope and naked eye observations) will be developed. At the Training Camp a Data Analysis exam along with a Round 3 theory paper will be sat. A team of five students (plus one reserve) will be selected for further training, including additional training camps in the summer.*

documentNotes.title: Important Formulae
documentNotes.statement:
You might find the diagram of an elliptical orbit below useful in solving some of the questions:

**Elements of an elliptic orbit**:

| | |
|---|---|
| $a = \mathbf{OA}\ (= \mathbf{OP})$ | semi-major axis |
| $b = \mathbf{OB}\ (= \mathbf{OC})$ | semi-minor axis |
| $e = \sqrt{1 - \frac{b^2}{a^2}}$ | eccentricity |
| $\mathbf{F}$ | focus |
| $\mathbf{PF} = a(1-e)$ | periapsis distance (shortest distance from $\mathbf{F}$) |
| $\mathbf{AF} = a(1+e)$ | apoapsis distance (longest distance from $\mathbf{F}$) |

**Kepler’s Third Law**: For an elliptical orbit, the square of the period, $T$, of an object about the focus is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis, $a$ (as defined above), such that

$$T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}a^3\,,$$

where $M$ is the total mass of the system (typically dominated by the central object) and $G$ is the universal gravitational constant.

**Vis-Viva Equation**: For an elliptical orbit, the speed $v$ of an object at a distance $r$ from the focus is related to the semi-major axis, $a$, total mass of the system, $M$, and universal gravitational constant, $G$, (as defined above), such that

$$v^2 = GM\left(\frac{2}{r} - \frac{1}{a}\right)\,.$$

**Magnitudes**: The apparent magnitudes of two objects, $m_1$ and $m_0$, are related to their apparent brightnesses, $b_1$ and $b_0$, via the formula

$$\frac{b_1}{b_0} = 10^{-0.4(m_1 - m_0)}\,.$$

The absolute magnitude of an object, $\mathcal{M}$, is the same as its apparent magnitude when viewed from 10 pc, hence the relationship between apparent and absolute magnitude and distance is

$$m - \mathcal{M} = 5\log\left(\frac{d}{10}\right),$$

where $d$ is measured in parsecs.

problems.title: Solar Analemma
problems.statement:
Plotting the position of the Sun in the sky at the same time every day, you get an interesting figure-of-eight shape known as an analemma (see Figure 1). For observers in the Northern hemisphere, you might expect to always see the Sun due South at midday, however on some days the Sun has already passed through that bearing and on others it needs a few more minutes before it gets there. This is due to two effects: the axial tilt of the Earth, and the fact the Earth’s orbit is not perfectly circular

The vertical co-ordinate of a point in the analemma is entirely determined by the Earth’s axial tilt. This is known as the solar declination, $\delta$, and varies sinusoidally throughout the year. The horizontal co-ordinate of a point in the analemma is determined by a combination of the Earth’s axial tilt and the eccentricity of the Earth’s orbit. Both of these individually vary sinusoidally, but the superposition of the two is no longer sinusoidal.

We will define $\alpha$ as the angle between due South and the Sun at local midday as seen from Oxford, where a positive value means the Sun has already passed through due South (so is on the right of the figure above) whilst a negative value means the Sun has yet to pass through due South. If $\alpha_{\mathrm{tilt}}$ is the contribution due to the axial tilt and $\alpha_{\mathrm{ecc}}$ is the contribution due to the Earth’s orbital eccentricity, then

$$\alpha = \alpha_{\mathrm{tilt}} + \alpha_{\mathrm{ecc}}\,.$$

If the angle of the axial tilt is $\varepsilon$ and the eccentricity of the Earth’s orbit is $e$, and we assume that both are small enough that the sinusoidal approximation of $\delta$, $\alpha_{\mathrm{tilt}}$, and $\alpha_{\mathrm{ecc}}$ apply, then we find the following boundary conditions:

- $\delta$ has a period of 1 year, an amplitude of $\varepsilon$, is maximum at the summer solstice (21st June) and minimum at the winter solstice (21st December)
- $\alpha_{\mathrm{tilt}}$ has a period of 0.5 years, an amplitude (in radians) of $\tan^2(\varepsilon/2)$, is zero at the solstices and the equinoxes (vernal equinox = 21st March, autumnal equinox = 21st September), and (using our sign convention) positive just after the vernal equinox
- $\alpha_{\mathrm{ecc}}$ has a period of 1 year, an amplitude (in radians) of $2e$, is zero at the perihelion (4th January) and the aphelion (6th July), and (using our sign convention) negative just after the perihelion

Given the $n^{\mathrm{th}}$ day of the year, a value can be calculated for $\delta$ and $\alpha$, and these are the co-ordinates for the analemma (it is drawn by these parametric equations). For the Earth, $\varepsilon = 23.44^{\circ}$ and $e = 0.0167$.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The analemma above was composed from images taken every few days at noon near the village of Callanish in the Outer Hebrides in Scotland. In the foreground are the Callanish Stones and the main photo was taken on the winter solstice (when the maximum angle the Sun reaches above the horizon is the lowest of the year, so is at the bottom of the analemma). Credit: Giuseppe Petricca.

The circled letters correspond to the same (unknown) day of each month (for example 5th Jan, 5th Feb, 5th March etc.). Credit: Bob Urschel.

The vertical axis has ticks labelled +15 degrees (top) and -15 degrees (bottom); the horizontal axis has ticks labelled -0h26m47s (left) and 0h18m56s (right). solution.statement:
**Q1 – Solar Analemma** **[35 marks]**

**a. (i)**

To convert from radians to minutes of time need to multiply by a factor of:

$$\frac{24\times60}{2\pi} = \frac{720}{\pi}$$ [1]

Putting the numbers into the given formula:

$\alpha_{tilt} = \tan^2\left(\frac{23.44^{\circ}}{2}\right) = 0.0430\ \mathrm{rad} = \boxed{9.86\ \text{minutes}}\ (= 9\ \mathrm{m}\ 51.8\ \mathrm{s})$ [1]

$\alpha_{ecc} = 2\times0.0167 = 0.0334\ \mathrm{rad} = \boxed{7.65\ \text{minutes}}\ (= 7\ \mathrm{m}\ 39.3\ \mathrm{s})$ [1] **[3]**

[If they only calculate both $\alpha$ in radians, award 1 mark. If they confuse the needed conversion with arcminutes (giving $\alpha_{\mathrm{tilt}}$ = 148’ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{ecc}}$ = 115’), lose first mark but give ecf. Conversion done correctly to just one $\alpha$ means max 2 marks. **Allow ecf for later parts**.]

**a. (ii)**

Considering the number of days between the winter solstice (21st Dec) and 1st Jan, which is a minimum, then

$$\boxed{\delta = -23.44^{\circ}\cos\left(2\pi\frac{n+10}{365}\right)}$$ [1] **[1]**

Since the winter solstice is a zero point, and $\alpha_{\mathrm{tilt}}$ is negative after it, with double the frequency of $\delta$:

$$\boxed{\alpha_{tilt} = -9.86\sin\left(4\pi\frac{n+10}{365}\right)}$$ [1] **[1]**

Since perihelion on 4th Jan is a zero point and $\alpha_{\mathrm{ecc}}$ is negative after it, with the same frequency as $\delta$

$$\boxed{\alpha_{ecc} = -7.65\sin\left(2\pi\frac{n-4}{365}\right)}$$ [1] **[1]**

[**Allow any equivalent expressions** in sin or cos, or using degrees inside the trigonometric functions. In these equations we are assuming midday on 1st Jan has n = 1 (so n = 0 & n = 365 at midday on 31st Dec) – do not penalise students for choosing a different zero point (e.g. midnight on 1st Jan) and hence getting slightly different additive terms to their n (allow ±1)]

**a. (iii)**

Correct shape, with rotational and reflectional symmetry and passing through (0,0) [1]

$\alpha$ axis labelled and extrema labelled as -9.86 mins and 9.86 mins (allow ecf from a)i)) [1]

$\delta$ axis labelled and extrema labelled as -23.44° and 23.44° [1]

**[3]**

**b.**

Part i) is the orange line [1] **[1]**

Part ii) is the blue line [1] **[1]**

Part iii) is the grey line

Has two maxima / minima (one bigger than the other) in ≈ the right place [1]

Largest maxima is larger amplitude than the lowest minima [1] **[2]**

[Allow ecf from earlier parts. Lose 0.5 marks for missing axes labels]

**c. (i)**

We can use the differential of $\alpha$ to find turning points, and then we know from the graph we want the ones near n ≈ 50 and n ≈ 300

$$\alpha = \alpha_{tilt} + \alpha_{ecc} = -9.86\sin\left(4\pi\frac{n+10}{365}\right) - 7.65\sin\left(2\pi\frac{n-4}{365}\right)$$

$$\therefore \frac{\mathrm{d}\alpha}{\mathrm{d}n} = -9.86\times\frac{4\pi}{365}\cos\left(4\pi\frac{n+10}{365}\right) - 7.65\times\frac{2\pi}{365}\cos\left(2\pi\frac{n-4}{365}\right)$$ [1]

Looking where d$\alpha$/dn = 0 (using any suitable method e.g. binary search) we find turning points in $\alpha$ at

$n = 44, 134, 207, 304$ [0.5 marks for each] [2]

We want the first and last values:

$n = 44 \therefore \text{date} = \boxed{13^{\text{th}}\ \text{Feb}}$ and $\alpha = \boxed{-14.31\ \text{mins}}$ [1]

$n = 304 \therefore \text{date} = \boxed{31^{\text{st}}\ \text{Oct}}$ and $\alpha = \boxed{+16.57\ \text{mins}}$ [1] **[5]**

[Do not penalise non-integer n. Allow n and dates consistent with their counting system (so may be different by ±1). For the final two marks it is 0.5 marks for a correct date and 0.5 marks for a correct $\alpha$]

[Our equation for alpha is known as the Equation of Time, and positive values mean that the Sun is ahead of the clock (so to the right of due south in the photo). Despite our approximations for the two components of $\alpha$, we are relatively close to the real extrema: -14.25 mins on 11th Feb and +16.42 mins on 3rd Nov]

**c. (ii)**

These correspond to when $\alpha$ = 0 [1]

Using any suitable method (e.g. binary search)

$n = 106, 164, 243, 359$ [0.5 marks for each] [2]

These correspond to the following dates:

$\boxed{16^{\text{th}}\ \text{Apr}}, \boxed{13^{\text{th}}\ \text{Jun}}, \boxed{31^{\text{st}}\ \text{Aug}}$ and $\boxed{25^{\text{th}}\ \text{Dec}}$ [0.5 marks for each] [2] **[5]**

[Do not penalise non-integer n. Allow n and dates consistent with their counting system (so may be different by ±1)]

[The real values are 15th Apr, 13th Jun, 1st Sep, and 25th Dec, so our approximations have done very well]

**c. (iii)**

We are told that $\alpha$ is small and can see from the photo that it is not near the solstices, so must be near the zero points in $\alpha$ far from the solstices i.e. 16th Apr and 31st Aug [1]

On 16th Apr $\delta$ is increasing, and on 31st Aug $\delta$ is decreasing. The know that $\delta$ at the crossover is equal on both dates (due to the equation for $\delta$ being double valued in the range of n) and between their two values of $\delta$ therefore the relevant dates must be **earlier** [1]

Using a suitable method (e.g. starting a binary search with these points as initial values)

$n = 106, \alpha = -0.10\ \text{mins}, \delta = 9.69^{\circ}$ $\qquad$ $n = 243, \alpha = -0.14\ \text{mins}, \delta = 8.20^{\circ}$

$n = 105, \alpha = -0.35\ \text{mins}, \delta = 9.32^{\circ}$ $\qquad$ $n = 242, \alpha = -0.47\ \text{mins}, \delta = 8.57^{\circ}$

$n = 104, \alpha = -0.61\ \text{mins}, \delta = 8.95^{\circ}$ $\qquad$ $n = 241, \alpha = -0.79\ \text{mins}, \delta = 8.95^{\circ}$

$n = 103, \alpha = -0.87\ \text{mins}, \delta = 8.57^{\circ}$ $\qquad$ $n = 240, \alpha = -1.10\ \text{mins}, \delta = 9.32^{\circ}$

[2]

$\therefore n = 104$ so date $= \boxed{14^{\text{th}}\ \text{Apr}}$ and n = 241 so date $= \boxed{29^{\text{th}}\ \text{Aug}}$ [1] **[5]**

[A wide variety of numerical methods might be employed here, although binary search close to the roots of $\alpha$ is probably the quickest. Allow ecf considerations as in earlier steps. Give 0.5 marks for each correct date]

[The real dates are 12th Apr and 29th Aug, so we have again done rather well]

**d. (i)**

The extrema in $\delta$ will be $\pm\varepsilon$ so just reading off the graph $\boxed{\varepsilon = 15^{\circ}}$ [1] **[1]**

**d. (ii)**

At the vernal equinox, $\delta$ = 0 and is increasing, so it must be $\boxed{\text{November}}$ [1] **[1]**

[Allow 0.5 marks for May, if it is clear it was chosen due to requiring $\delta$ = 0]

**d. (iii)**

With the information in the previous two parts, we can create an equation for $\alpha$

The component due to eccentricity has the same general form

$$\alpha_{ecc} = -2e\sin\left(2\pi\frac{n-4}{365}\right)$$ [0.5]

Using the earlier equations for $\alpha_{\mathrm{tilt}}$

$$\alpha_{tilt} = \tan^2\left(\frac{15^{\circ}}{2}\right) = 0.0173\ \mathrm{rad} = 3.97\ \text{minutes}$$ [0.5]

Since the vernal equinox is now 21st November (30 days earlier than the winter solstice used to be), our sinusoidal equation can be modified to

$$\alpha_{tilt} = 3.97\sin\left(4\pi\frac{n+40}{365}\right)$$ [Accept equivalent forms] [0.5]

Putting in data for one extremum (e.g. -26 mins 47 secs = -26.783 mins) and knowing it is a turning point (so $\frac{\mathrm{d}\alpha}{\mathrm{d}n} = 0$) gives us two equations:

$-2e\sin\left(2\pi\frac{n_1-4}{365}\right) + 3.97\sin\left(4\pi\frac{n_1+40}{365}\right) = -26.783$ ①

$-2e\times\frac{2\pi}{365}\cos\left(2\pi\frac{n_1-4}{365}\right) + 3.97\times\frac{4\pi}{365}\cos\left(4\pi\frac{n_1+40}{365}\right) = 0$ ② [0.5]

Combining ① and ② to eliminate e, gives the equation

$$\tan\left(2\pi\frac{n_1-4}{365}\right) - \frac{1}{2}\tan\left(4\pi\frac{n_1+40}{365}\right) - \frac{26.783}{3.97\times2\cos\left(4\pi\frac{n_1+40}{365}\right)} = 0$$ [1]

Using an appropriate numerical method to solve it for $n_1$, the only valid values in the allowed region are

$n_1 = 96$ or $278$ [1]

Recognising that the relevant extremum is around April, $n_1$ = 96 is the correct one to choose.

Putting this into either ① or ② leads to $\boxed{e = 0.0498}$ [1] **[5]**

[Using the other extremum gets $n_2 = 92$ or $274$ and so recognising the latter is the correct one to use gives $\boxed{e = 0.0499}$. The method outlined here works in general, however in this specific case an alternative (much shorter) method will work; $\alpha_{\mathrm{tilt}}$ has minima at n = 97 and 279, which almost exactly coincide with the turning points of $\alpha_{\mathrm{ecc}}$ at n = 95 (min) and 278 (max). Consequently, by considering how the graph of $\alpha_{\mathrm{ecc}}$, $\alpha_{\mathrm{tilt}}$ and $\alpha$ would look, it is clear that $-2e - 3m57 \approx -26m47$ and $2e - 3m57 \approx 18m56$. Taking the average of the modulus of the extrema in $\alpha$, and assuming that is 2e gives $\boxed{e = 0.0499}$. Students that use this approach to take advantage of the greatly simplifying phase relationship between $\alpha_{\mathrm{ecc}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{tilt}}$ receive full credit (same first 1.5 marks, 1 mark for turning points, 0.5 marks for recognising the consequences of the tuning points being close together, 1 mark for setting up equations, 1 mark for final answer). Those whose working implies they did not recognise this was a special case (and hence suggest this method would always work) get 1 mark only for a correct final answer]

problems.title: Wolf-Rayet Dust Shells
problems.statement:
Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars are some of the hottest stars known, with very strong stellar winds causing considerable mass to the be lost to the interstellar medium (ISM). In binary systems between a WR star and a very large O or B spectral class star, where their strong stellar winds collide can create the conditions for the formation of dust which goes on to enrich the ISM.

The WR140 system consists of a WR and an O star which produce dust very regularly when the two stars are close together, around periastron. They are in a highly elliptical orbit ($e = 0.8993$) with a period of $2895$ days. Once far from the stars, these dust shells move through space at a remarkably constant speed as indicated by the regularity of the shells in the recent image taken with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), shown above in Figure 3. An artist’s impression of the two stars in the system and the orbit (in the reference frame of the WR star) is shown in Figure 4 below.

figures.caption: Figure 3: *Left:* A view of the WR140 binary system taken with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) in July 2022, showing clearly at least 17 nested dust shells. Credit: NASA/ESA/CSA/STScI/JPL-Caltech. *Right:* A radial plot along the image in the three mid infrared JWST filters used corresponding to 7.7, 15 and 21 µm, as well as the model of the dust production. The peaks correspond to each shell. Shells 2 and 17 are indicated on the model and the median shell separation is shown by the grey vertical lines. The projected distance is given in arcseconds. Credit: Lau et al. (2022).
figures.alt: Left: JWST infrared image of WR140 — a bright central star with many nested, roughly circular pinkish dust shells on a dark star field. Right: log plot of Normalized flux (0.0001 to 1,000) against Projected distance from WR 140 (″) from 0 to 50. Three peaked curves: F770W (×10) blue, F1500W (×100) green, F2100W (×1,000) red-brown, plus a dashed black Model curve; grey vertical lines mark the median shell separation. On the model curve the peak near 4″ is labelled 2 and the peak near 44″ is labelled 17.

figures.caption: Figure 4: *Left:* The relative size of the Sun, upper left, compared to the two stars in the system WR140. The O-type star is $\sim 30\,M_{\odot}$, while its companion is $\sim 10\,M_{\odot}$. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech. *Right:* The projected orbital configuration of WR 140 in the reference frame of the WR star. The red solid region around the periastron passage is where the O star is when dust is being formed. Credit: Lau et al. (2022).
figures.alt: Left: artist's impression on a black background of a tiny Sun (upper left, labelled Sun), a bright white Wolf-Rayet Star surrounded by blue turbulent wind, and a larger pale blue O Star. Right: dashed elliptical orbit tilted on the page; the WR star (small light-blue dot labelled WR) sits near the upper-left end, where a red solid arc marks part of the orbit; the O star (blue dot labelled O) lies at the lower right with a dark arrow showing the direction of motion.

figures.caption: Figure 5: *Left:* The collision of stellar winds between the WR and O star creates a conical shock front in which the conditions are right for dust production. This cone is shown when at periastron in the reference frame of the WR star, although dust production is not limited to periastron so the cone can have a wide range of orientations. The place where the shock front is closest to the WR star is known as the stagnation point. *Right:* Close to the stars no dust is made in the conical shock fronts, however once far enough away the dust forms and is optically thick so experiences strong radiation pressure accelerating it. Eventually a distance is reached where the dust becomes optically thin and the acceleration decreases. Credit: Han et al. (2022).
figures.alt: Panel a: points WR and OB on a dashed horizontal line; a blue shaded hyperbolic cone opens to the right around OB, labelled Conical shock front, with an ellipse around it marked Azimuthal direction; a dashed curved path with an arrow is labelled Orbital direction. Panel b: WR and OB close together on a dashed line, with a blue curved band to the right; regions labelled No dust (inside), Optically thick dust (the band) and Optically thin dust (beyond a dotted outer arc).

Diagram of an elliptical orbit from the Important Formulae page: ellipse with centre O, focus F (blue dot), periapsis P and apoapsis A at the ends of the major axis, B and C at the ends of the minor axis; dashed semi-axes labelled a and b.

parts.label: a. (i)
parts.statement:
Take the distance to the system to be $1.64$ kpc.

By taking measurements from Figure 3, show that the average radial expansion velocity between shells 2 to 17 is $\sim 2600$ km s$^{-1}$. [1 arcsecond $= 1''$ is a measurement of angle, where $3600'' = 1^{\circ}$.]

parts.label: a. (ii)
parts.statement: Shell 1 was observed by JWST on 27th July 2022 to be $1.63''$ away from the central stars. It was formed during the last periastron passage of the O star, which (as viewed from Earth) took place in December 2016. Taking light travel time into account, in what year was the periastron passage responsible for shell 17?
parts.statementAfter:
The average radial expansion velocity of shell 1 is less than that seen for shells 2 to 17, suggesting a mechanism accelerates the dust up to that speed from some lower speed resultant from the bow shock between the two colliding stellar winds. A prime candidate is radiation pressure, where photons deposit all of their momentum onto an optically thick dust cloud, before it moves too far from the original stars and becomes optically thin (so the transfer of momentum becomes less and less efficient) as shown in the right panel of Figure 5.

The radiation force, $F_{\mathrm{rad}}$, experienced by a single dust grain at a distance $r$ is given as

$$F_{\mathrm{rad}} = \sigma_g\frac{L_{\mathrm{bin}}}{4\pi r^2 c}\,,$$

where $\sigma_g$ is the cross-sectional area of the dust grain, $c$ is the speed of light and $L_{\mathrm{bin}}$ is the combined luminosity of the binary system. Han et al. (2022) suggest the following acceleration model to match the observations:

$$a(t) = \begin{cases} 0 & 0 \le r < r_{inner} \\ a_{\max} & r_{inner} \le r < r_{outer} \\ \frac{a_{\max}r_{outer}^2}{r^2} & r \ge r_{outer} \end{cases}$$

Here, $r_{inner}$ is the inner radius of the optically thick dust shell and $r_{outer}$ is the distance at which it becomes optically thin. $a_{\max}$ is the constant acceleration experienced by the dust whilst optically thick, and is equal to the acceleration of a dust grain by radiation pressure at $r = r_{outer}$.

parts.label: b. (i)
parts.statement:
In the Han et al. (2022) model they use $r_{inner} = 50$ au, $r_{outer} = 220$ au, and assume spherical dust grains with a radius of $40$ nm and density $1.6$ g cm$^{-3}$, as well as a dust-to-gas ratio of $0.019$. Take the apparent magnitude of the system (after correcting for substantial extinction by the dust shells and the general ISM) as $m = 0.426$, and you are given the absolute magnitude of the Sun is $\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 4.74$.

Show that $a_{\max}$ is $\sim 940$ km s$^{-1}$ yr$^{-1}$.

answer.note: Using the exact factor m_dust/m_tot = 0.01865 gives 924 km s^-1 yr^-1, also accepted.

parts.label: b. (ii)
parts.statement: Hence, sketch $a(r)$ from $0 \le r \le 2500$ au.

parts.label: b. (iii)
parts.statement: Given shell 1 is measured to be moving at $2540$ km s$^{-1}$, calculate the initial speed of the gas streaming away from the stars in the conical shock front, $v_0$, before it experiences the acceleration due to radiation pressure.
parts.statementAfter: The stellar winds from each star are initially thermally accelerated up to a terminal velocity, $v_{\infty}$, following the relationship $v(r) = v_{\infty}(1 - R_{\star}/r)$, where $R_{\star}$ is the radius of the star. The shape of the conical shock front is well approximated as a hyperbolic cross-section so long as the speed of each star’s wind at the shock front is $\approx v_{\infty}$ where they meet. This is true for much of the orbit and the cone, however due to the extreme eccentricity of the WR140 system at periapsis it may not hold close to the stagnation point (the closest the cone gets to the WR star, as seen in Figure 5).

parts.label: c. (i)
parts.statement:
The measured semi-major axis of the WR140 system from radio interferometry is $8.82$ milliarcseconds. Investigation of spectral lines shows that for the O star $v_{\infty,O} = 3100$ km s$^{-1}$ and for the WR star $v_{\infty,WR} = 2800$ km s$^{-1}$, and measurements of X-ray absorption lead to suggested mass loss rates of $\dot{M}_O = 3.7\times10^{-7}\,M_{\odot}\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ and $\dot{M}_{WR} = 1.7\times10^{-5}\,M_{\odot}\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ respectively for each star. In the shock front, the pressure from each stellar wind is balanced. Considering the system at periapsis:

Show that the distance from the O star to the stagnation point is

$$r_O = \frac{\sqrt{\eta}}{1+\sqrt{\eta}}r_{peri}\,,$$

where $\eta$ is the ratio of the momenta of the two stellar winds, $\eta \equiv \frac{p_O}{p_{WR}}$ and $r_{peri}$ is the separation between the stars at periapsis.

parts.label: c. (ii)
parts.statement: Hence, calculate $r_O$ in au.

parts.label: c. (iii)
parts.statement: Taking the WR star to be approximately 2 times more luminous than the O star, and the effective surface temperatures of the stars to be $T_{\mathrm{eff,O}} = 35$ kK and $T_{\mathrm{eff,WR}} = 60$ kK, calculate the radius of each star in solar units.

parts.label: c. (iv)
parts.statement: Hence, determine for which star(s) the assumption of $v \approx v_{\infty}$ at the stagnation point is reasonable, and suggest (if any) the change in the position of the stagnation point taking in the real values of $v$ at $r_O$.

answer.value: Only for the WR star (v ≈ 0.97 v∞,WR, while the O-star wind has only 0.55 v∞,O); the stagnation point will be even closer to the O star.

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: The conditions for dust production turn on when the stars get within $\approx 7.9$ au of each other, corresponding to the solid red region in the right panel of Figure 4. A line from the WR star to the start of dust production region makes an angle of $45^{\circ}$ with the semi-major axis. By using Kepler’s second law, or otherwise, estimate the rough duration of dust production during each orbit. Give your answer in years to 2 decimal places, making any simplifying assumptions clear. [Hint: Kepler’s second law states that the area swept out by one object orbiting another is equal in the same amount of time, such that $\mathrm{d}A/\mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{constant} = \pi ab/T$ where $T$ is the period]

answer.note: The marking scheme accepts any justified method giving 0.60–0.70 years.

solution.statement:
**Q2 – Wolf-Rayet Dust Shells** **[40 marks]**

**a. (i)**

Measuring from the graph, the average spacing between shells is 2.67” [1]

[Expect to see candidates realise that 40” covers the 15 intervals from shell 2 to 17, and hence the average separation is 40”/15 = 2.67”. Allow ±0.03” and ecf on all subsequent parts of the question accordingly]

Using the small angle approximation (with the angle converted into radians), the distance between shells implied by their average angular spacing is

$$d_{shell} = d_{system}\tan\theta \approx d_{system}\theta = 1.64\times\left(\frac{2.67}{3600}\times\frac{2\pi}{360}\right)$$

$$= 2.12\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{kpc} = 6.56\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{km}$$ [1]

Given the period is 2895 days and converting it to seconds,

$$v_{shell} = \frac{d_{shell}}{T} = \frac{6.56\times10^{11}}{2895\times24\times60\times60} = 2622.6\ldots = \boxed{2620\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}}$$ [1] **[3]**

[Given it is a ‘show that’, it must have $\geq$ 3 s.f. in final answer]

**a. (ii)**

From shell 1 to shell 17 is 16 intervals, so in years

$$\Delta t = 16\times\left(\frac{2895}{365}\right) = 126.9\ \mathrm{yrs}$$ [1]

[Accept use of 365.25 days in a year]

The light travel time from the system is

$$t_{system} = \frac{d_{system}}{c} = \frac{1.24\times1000\times3.09\times10^{16}}{3.00\times10^{8}} = 1.69\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{s} = 5356.4\ \mathrm{yrs}$$ [1]

Given that December 2016 is approximately decimalised as 2016.9, and that 1 BC goes to 1 AD with no year zero, then the year it was created is

$$2016.9 - (126.9 + 5356.4) - 1 = -3467.4 = (\text{July})\ \boxed{3467\ \text{BC}}$$ [1] **[3]**

[Accept use of 2016 instead of 2016.9, and not skipping year 0, giving an allowance of ±2 years on the final answer]

**b. (i)**

First we can find the absolute magnitude of the system

$$\mathcal{M} = m - 5\log\left(\frac{d_{system}}{10}\right) = 0.426 - 5\log\left(\frac{1.64\times10^{3}}{10}\right) = -10.65$$ [1]

By comparison with the Sun we can turn this into a luminosity

$$L = 10^{\frac{\mathcal{M}-\mathcal{M}_{\odot}}{-2.5}}L_{\odot} = 10^{\frac{-10.65-4.74}{-2.5}}L_{\odot} = 1.43\times10^{6}\,L_{\odot} = 5.50\times10^{32}\ \mathrm{W}$$ [1]

From Newton’s 2nd Law

$$a_{max} = \frac{F_{rad}}{m_{tot}} = \frac{F_{rad}}{m_{dust}}\times\frac{m_{dust}}{m_{tot}} \approx \frac{F_{rad}}{m_{dust}}\times\frac{m_{dust}}{m_{gas}} = \frac{\sigma_g}{m_{dust}}\frac{L_{bin}}{4\pi r_{outer}^2c}\times\frac{m_{dust}}{m_{gas}}$$

$$= \frac{\pi r_{dust}^2}{\rho_{dust}\times\frac{4}{3}\pi r_{dust}^3}\frac{L_{bin}}{4\pi r_{outer}^2c}\times\frac{m_{dust}}{m_{gas}} = \frac{3L_{bin}}{16\rho_{dust}r_{dust}\pi r_{outer}^2c}\times\frac{m_{dust}}{m_{gas}}$$ [1]

$$\therefore a_{max} = \frac{3\times5.50\times10^{32}}{16\times1600\times40\times10^{-9}\times\pi\times(220\times1.50\times10^{11})^2\times3.00\times10^{8}}\times0.019$$

$$= 2.99\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$$ [1]

$$= \boxed{941\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,yr^{-1}}}$$ [1] **[5]**

[Given it is a ‘show that’, it must have $\geq$ 3 s.f. in final answer. Final mark is for correct unit conversion. Give full credit for the use of the exact corrective factor $\frac{m_{dust}}{m_{tot}} = \frac{m_{dust}}{m_{dust}+m_{gas}} = \frac{1}{1+m_{gas}/m_{dust}} = 0.01865$, leading to $a_{\max} = 2.93\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} = \boxed{924\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,yr^{-1}}}$. Forgetting about the use of the dust-to-gas ratio gives $a_{\max} = 1.57\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} = 49554\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,yr^{-1}}$ and scores 4 marks max. If no attempt at the algebraic simplification, the third mark can be gained for either a correct $m_{\mathrm{dust}}$ (= $4.29\times10^{-19}$ kg) **or** $\sigma_{\mathrm{g}}$ (= $5.03\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m^2}$)]

**b. (ii)**

Zero from $0 \le r < 50$ au

**and** flat section at ~940 km s$^{-1}$ yr$^{-1}$ from $50 \le r < 220$ au [1]

Following 1/r$^2$ shape from $220 \le r \le 2500$ au [1] **[2]**

[Lose 1 mark if the axes are not labelled, or a scale on either axis is missing. The horizontal axis does not need to be to scale, so long as key values indicated. Expect to see a (not to scale) sketch like the one below]

**b. (iii)**

The work done by the radiative force on the dust is equal to its change in KE

$$\Delta KE = \frac{1}{2}m_{dust}v_{shell1}^2 - \frac{1}{2}m_{dust}v_0^2$$

$$= \int_{r_{inner}}^{r_{shell1}}F(r)\,\mathrm{d}r = m_{dust}\int_{r_{inner}}^{r_{shell1}}a(r)\,\mathrm{d}r$$

$$\therefore \frac{1}{2}v_0^2 = \frac{1}{2}v_{shell1}^2 - \int_{r_{inner}}^{r_{shell1}}a(r)\,\mathrm{d}r$$ [1]

[This formula could also be arrived at by generalising the SUVAT equation $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ into $v^2 = u^2 + 2\int a(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$]

In a. ii we were told the angular separation of shell 1 from the star, so

$$r_{shell1} = 1.64\times\left(\frac{1.63}{3600}\times\frac{2\pi}{360}\right) = 1.30\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{kpc} = 4.00\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m}$$ [1]

[This corresponds to 2670 au. If they use $r_{\mathrm{shell1}}$ = 2500 au in the subsequent integration lose only this mark (so get max 4 marks)]

Evaluating the integral with everything in SI units

$$\int_{r_{inner}}^{r_{shell1}}a(r)\,\mathrm{d}r = \int_{r_{inner}}^{r_{outer}}a_{max}\,\mathrm{d}r + \int_{r_{outer}}^{r_{shell1}}\frac{a_{max}r_{outer}^2}{r^2}\,\mathrm{d}r$$

$$= [a_{max}\times(r_{outer}-r_{inner})] + \left[-a_{max}r_{outer}^2\left(\frac{1}{r_{shell1}^2}-\frac{1}{r_{outer}^2}\right)\right]$$ [1]

$$= [2.99\times10^{-2}\times(220-50)\times1.50\times10^{11}]$$

$$+[-2.99\times10^{-2}\times(220\times1.50\times10^{11})^2\times\left(\frac{1}{(4.00\times10^{14})^2}-\frac{1}{(220\times1.50\times10^{11})^2}\right)$$

$$= 7.61\times10^{11} + 9.04\times10^{11}$$

$$= 1.67\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$$ [1]

[0.5 marks for either correctly evaluated integral (flat section or curved section)]

We can now evaluate $v_0$

$$\therefore v_0 = \sqrt{v_{shell1}^2 - 2\int_{r_{inner}}^{r_{shell1}}a(r)\,\mathrm{d}r} = \sqrt{(2540\times10^3)^2 - 2\times1.67\times10^{12}}$$

$$= 1.77\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} = \boxed{1770\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}}$$ [1] **[5]**

[Accept answer in m s$^{-1}$ or km s$^{-1}$ for final mark. Allow ecf from their $a_{\max}$]

**c. (i)**

The ram pressure is $p_{ram} = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{\dot{p}}{A}$ where $\dot{p}$ is the rate of change of momentum, so at the stagnation point (assuming spherically symmetric stellar winds)

$$\frac{\dot{p}_O}{4\pi r_O^2} = \frac{\dot{p}_{WR}}{4\pi(r_{peri}-r_O)^2}$$ [1]

$$\therefore \frac{\dot{p}_O}{\dot{p}_{WR}} = \frac{r_O^2}{(r_{peri}-r_O)^2}$$

But since $\eta = \frac{p_O}{p_{WR}} = \frac{\dot{p}_O}{\dot{p}_{WR}}$ then $\eta = \frac{r_O^2}{(r_{peri}-r_O)^2} \therefore \sqrt{\eta} = \frac{r_O}{r_{peri}-r_O}$ [1] **[2]**

This can then be rearranged to give the required formula

$$\sqrt{\eta}(r_{peri}-r_O) = r_O \therefore \sqrt{\eta}r_{peri} = (1+\sqrt{\eta})r_O \therefore r_O = \frac{\sqrt{\eta}}{1+\sqrt{\eta}}r_{peri}$$

[The first mark is for setting up the problem algebraically **or** for a helpful diagram. The second mark is for correctly introducing $\eta$ **and** having convincing algebra to the final answer (since it was given, no standalone mark for the final expression)]

**c. (ii)**

First, we can calculate $\eta$

$$\eta = \frac{p_O}{p_{WR}} = \frac{\dot{p}_O}{\dot{p}_{WR}} = \frac{\dot{M}_Ov_{\infty,O}}{\dot{M}_{WR}v_{\infty,WR}} = \frac{3.7\times10^{-7}\times3100}{1.7\times10^{-5}\times2800} = 0.024$$ [1]

We can also calculate the semi-major axis, and then use the given eccentricity to get the periapsis distance

$$a = 1.64\times\left(\frac{8.82\times10^{-3}}{3600}\times\frac{2\pi}{360}\right) = 7.01\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{kpc} = 14.44\ \mathrm{au}$$ [1]

$$r_{peri} = a(1-e) = 14.44\times(1-0.8993) = 1.45\ \mathrm{au}$$ [1]

Putting it all into the formula of the previous part

$$r_O = \frac{\sqrt{\eta}}{1+\sqrt{\eta}}r_{peri} = \frac{\sqrt{0.024}}{1+\sqrt{0.024}}\times1.45 = \boxed{0.195\ \mathrm{au}}$$ [1] **[4]**

[Must be in au for the final mark, although a and $r_{\mathrm{peri}}$ might be given in metres ($2.17\times10^{12}$ m and $2.18\times10^{11}$ m respectively)]

**c. (iii)**

We can split up the luminosity calculated earlier in b. i.

$$L_{WR} = \frac{2}{3}L_{bin} = \frac{2}{3}\times1.43\times10^{6} = 9.53\times10^{5}\,L_{\odot} = 3.67\times10^{32}\ \mathrm{W}$$ [0.5]

$$L_O = \frac{1}{3}L_{bin} = \frac{1}{3}\times1.43\times10^{6} = 4.77\times10^{5}\,L_{\odot} = 1.83\times10^{32}\ \mathrm{W}$$ [0.5]

Using the Stephan-Boltzmann law

$$R_{WR} = \sqrt{\frac{L_{WR}}{4\pi\sigma T_{WR}^4}} = \sqrt{\frac{3.67\times10^{32}}{4\pi\times5.67\times10^{8}\times(60\times10^3)^4}} = 6.30\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{m} = \boxed{9.06\,R_{\odot}}$$ [1] **[1.5]**

$$R_O = \sqrt{\frac{L_O}{4\pi\sigma T_O^4}} = \sqrt{\frac{1.83\times10^{32}}{4\pi\times5.67\times10^{8}\times(35\times10^3)^4}} = 1.31\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m} = \boxed{18.82\,R_{\odot}}$$ [1] **[1.5]**

[Score max 2 out of 3 if their final answer is not in $R_{\odot}$.

Give full credit if they assume $T_{\odot} \approx 5780\ \mathrm{K}$ and so use $R = \sqrt{\frac{L/L_{\odot}}{(T/T_{\odot})^4}}R_{\odot}$ for calculations]

[This matches up well with the scale of the stars in Figure 4 in the paper, showing these are both large, very hot stars.]

**c. (iv)**

Using the given formula:

$$v_{r_O} = v_{\infty,O}\left(1-\frac{R_O}{r_O}\right) = \left(1-\frac{1.31\times10^{10}}{0.195\times1.50\times10^{11}}\right)v_{\infty,O} = 0.55v_{\infty,O}$$ [1]

$$v_{r_{WR}} = v_{\infty,WR}\left(1-\frac{R_{WR}}{r_{peri}-r_O}\right) = \left(1-\frac{6.30\times10^{9}}{(1.45-0.195)\times1.50\times10^{11}}\right)v_{\infty,WR} = 0.97v_{\infty,WR}$$ [1]

So $v \approx v_{\infty}$ is only a reasonable assumption for the WR star (at periapsis) [0.5]

This means the stagnation point will be even closer to the O star [0.5] **[3]**

[Do not allow bald statement that it is a reasonable assumption for the WR star without evidence of calculation]

**d.**

From Kepler’s 2nd law, $\frac{\text{area of shaded section}}{\text{total area of the ellipse}} = \frac{\text{time spent in shaded section}}{\text{period of the orbit}}$ [1]

We can use approximate geometry to calculate this area e.g. breaking the non-shaded section up into a triangle (ABS) and trapezium (ABDC) sat within a half-ellipse: [1]

Given the symmetry, angle $\angle ASB = 2\times45^{\circ} = 90^{\circ}$

$$\therefore \text{area of triangle } ABS = \frac{1}{2}\times7.9^2 = 31.2\ \mathrm{au}^2$$ [1]

We can also use Pythagoras’ theorem to get the length AB

$$AB = \sqrt{7.9^2+7.9^2} = 11.2\ \mathrm{au}$$ [1]

The height of the trapezium

$$h = a - r_{peri} - 7.9\cos45^{\circ} = 14.44 - 1.45 - 5.59 = 7.41\ \mathrm{au}$$ [1]

The length of CD is the minor axis (= 2b), which can be calculated from rearranging the formula given at the beginning of the paper

$$e = \sqrt{1-\frac{b^2}{a^2}} \therefore b = a\sqrt{1-e^2} = 14.44\times\sqrt{1-0.8993^2} = 6.3\ \mathrm{au}$$ [1]

Hence, the area of the trapezium

$$\text{area } ABDC = \frac{1}{2}(AB+CD)h = \frac{1}{2}(11.2+(2\times6.3))\times7.41 = 88.2\ \mathrm{au}^2$$ [1]

Finally, the area of the half-ellipse (to the left of CD)

$$\text{area half-ellipse} = \frac{1}{2}\pi ab = \frac{1}{2}\pi\times14.44\times6.3 = 143.4\ \mathrm{au}^2$$ [1]

The area of the shaded section is therefore

$$\text{shaded area} = \text{area of half-ellipse} - (\text{area ABS} + \text{area ABDC})$$

$$= 143.4 - (31.2+88.2) = 24.0\ \mathrm{au}^2$$ [1]

Finally, applying Kepler’s 2nd law

$$t = \frac{\text{shaded area}}{\text{total area}}\times T = \frac{24.0}{2\times143.4}\times2895 = 0.084\times2895 = 242\ \text{days} = \boxed{0.66\ \text{yrs}}$$ [1] **[10]**

[Must be in years and to 2 d.p. for the final mark. A wide variety of approaches are possible, so award marks based upon sensible choices of shapes to evaluate the area of. The first mark is for realising how to apply Kepler’s 2nd law in this context, the second mark is for a clear approach to break the ellipse up into shapes (ideally with a diagram – and not necessarily the triangle and trapezium used here), and the final mark is for the final answer – all other marks are available for sensible areas and lengths relevant to their method. Accept any method that gives a value of 0.60-0.70 years so long as the justification is clear]

[The more exact way to work this out is using our knowledge of anomalies, although some approximations were made to simplify the geometric case in terms of the given length and angle. Assuming the angle to be correct, leads to a true anomaly $\nu = 180^{\circ} - 45^{\circ} = 135^{\circ}$. Given this and the quoted eccentricity and semi-major axis, the real length AS is 7.6 au, and utilising Kepler’s equation to get the time for $-135^{\circ} \le \nu \le 135^{\circ}$ gives 0.633 years. Alternatively, assuming the length AS = 7.9 au to be correct, leads to a real true anomaly of 136.3°, and when looking at the time to travel from $-136.3^{\circ} \le \nu \le 136.3^{\circ}$ gives 0.671 years. Students using this approach (rather than areas of shapes) get full credit. However the problem is approached, it is clear that dust is only produced on a relatively short time frame, which is why each shell has such contrast.]

problems.title: Planetary Migration in Protoplanetary Discs
problems.statement: Young, Earth-like planets interact with the protoplanetary discs in which they form, and as a result migrate to different orbital radii. The aim of this question is to quantify this migration in a simple model. We shall think of protoplanetary discs as consisting of nested circular orbits of gas and dust around a central star. For a thin disc (with small vertical extent), we assign to the disc a surface density (or mass per unit area) $\Sigma$, and semi-thickness $H$, which in general vary over the disc’s extent. The disc’s ‘aspect ratio’ at radius $r$ from the central star is denoted $h = H/r$. This question is concerned with the migration of ‘small’ planets, such that $M_p/M_{\star} = q \ll h^3$.

figures.caption: Figure 6: *Left:* ALMA image of the young star HL Tau and its protoplanetary disk. This image of planet formation reveals multiple rings and gaps that herald the presence of emerging planets as they sweep their orbits clear of dust and gas. Credit: ALMA (NRAO/ESO/NAOJ) / C. Brogan, B. Saxton (NRAO/AUI/NSF). *Right:* A small planet orbits whilst embedded in a protoplanetary disc, exciting a 1-armed spiral density wave. Credit: Frédéric Masset.
figures.alt: Left: ALMA image of HL Tau — an inclined elliptical orange-yellow disc on black, with a bright centre and concentric bright rings separated by dark gaps. Right: simulation of a face-on orange disc with a black central hole; a small bright spot (the planet) to the right of the hole launches a single thin bright spiral arm winding around the disc.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement:
Consider a planet of mass $M_p$ in a circular orbit of radius $r_p$ about a star of mass $M_{\star}$, with $M_p/M_{\star} = q \ll 1$. Show that it has angular velocity and angular momentum about the central star given by:

$$\Omega_p = \sqrt{\frac{GM_{\star}}{r_p^3}}, \quad L = M_p\sqrt{GM_{\star}r_p}$$

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Consider now a rotationally symmetric disc with surface density profile $\Sigma = \Sigma_0\,(r/r_0)^{-3/2}$, and outer radius $r_{\mathrm{out}} = 9r_0$. Find the mass of the disc $M_{\mathrm{disc}}$ in terms of $\Sigma_0$ and $r_0$ assuming its inner radius $r_{\mathrm{in}} \ll r_0$.
parts.statementAfter:
Since the planet is assumed small ($q \ll h^3$), its interaction with the gas in the disc constitutes the excitation of a spiral density wave, and redistribution of matter in the co-orbital region (that is, matter orbiting at radii $r \approx r_p$), as shown in Figure 6. The resulting non-uniform density distribution induced in the disc exerts a net gravitational force, and hence a torque on the planet, which has been estimated using analytical methods. This torque, $\Gamma$, acts to change the planet’s angular momentum, and hence its orbital radius, causing it to ‘migrate’, via:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}L}{\mathrm{d}t} = \Gamma$$

It is convenient to write the torque in terms of the reference value

$$\Gamma_0 = \left(\frac{q}{h}\right)^2\Sigma_p r_p^4\Omega_p^2\,.$$

parts.label: c.
parts.statement:
From 2-dimensional steady fluid-dynamical disc models, it is predicted that the total torque $\Gamma$ has two main contributions: from the spiral wave, the ‘Lindblad torque’, $\Gamma_L$, and from the co-orbital region, the ‘Corotation torque’, $\Gamma_C$. For a disc of uniform entropy ($\mathrm{d}s = 0$), and with surface density profile $\Sigma \propto r^{-\alpha}$, and pressure profile $P \propto r^{-\delta}$, Tanaka et al. (2002) and Paardekooper & Papaloizou (2009) find these torques are given by:

$$\Gamma_L = (-3.20 + 0.86\alpha - 2.33\delta)\Gamma_0$$

$$\Gamma_C = 5.97\,(1.5 - \alpha)\,\Gamma_0$$

We assume the gas in the disc obeys the ideal gas law, so that:

$$\frac{P}{\Sigma T} = \text{constant}, \quad \mathrm{d}s = \text{constant}\times\left(\frac{1}{\gamma-1}\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{T} - \frac{\mathrm{d}\Sigma}{\Sigma}\right)\,,$$

where $T$ is the absolute temperature and $\gamma$ is the adiabatic index (the ratio of the heat capacity at constant pressure to the heat capacity at constant volume). Show that for a disc of uniform entropy,

$$\Gamma = \Gamma_L + \Gamma_C = (5.76 - (5.11 + 2.33\gamma)\alpha)\,\Gamma_0\,.$$

*[Hint: if* $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{y} = \lambda\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x}$*, then* $y \propto x^{\lambda}$*.]*

parts.label: d.
parts.statement:
Assume the disc model from part b. with $h = \mathrm{const}$. Find the time taken for the orbital radius of the planet to halve from initial radius $r_0$. Take $\gamma = 1.4$, and give your answer in terms of the migration timescale,

$$t_{\mathrm{m}} = \frac{1}{h}\left(\frac{h^3}{q}\right)\frac{M_{\star}}{M_{\mathrm{disc}}}\tau_0\,,$$

where $\tau_0$ is the orbital period at radius $r_0$.

parts.label: e.
parts.statement: If the disc has mass $M_{\mathrm{disc}} = 0.01M_{\star}$ and aspect ratio $h = 0.05$, and if $q = 5\times10^{-6}$ and $\tau_0 = 10$ years, find the elapsed time in years for the migration described in part d. to occur. Is this a feasible mechanism for planetary migration given the lifetime of the disc is roughly $10$ Myr?

answer.note: Yes — this is well within the 10 Myr disc lifetime, so it is a feasible mechanism.

parts.label: f.
parts.statement:
Whilst the planet excites a spiral density wave over the whole disc, in fact the dominant contribution to the torque from the spiral is from only a small neighbourhood around the planet, so that $\alpha$ may be replaced by

$$-\frac{r_p}{\Sigma_p}\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}\Sigma}{\mathrm{d}r}\right|_p\,.$$

Near the inner radius of the disc, the surface density departs from the above power-law behaviour and smoothly decreases to $0$. Does the migration stop before the planet reaches the disc’s inner radius?

answer.value: Yes — the migration does halt before the inner edge of the disc (α changes from 1.5 to negative values, so it passes through α_crit where Γ = 0).

problems.statementAfterParts:
**Helpful equations:**

The moment of inertia, $I$, of a point mass $m$ moving in a circle of radius $r$ is $I = mr^2$.

The angular momentum, $L$, of a spinning object with an angular velocity of $\Omega$ is $L = I\Omega = r\times p$, where $p$ is the linear momentum of a point particle a distance $r$ from the axis of rotation.

solution.statement:
**Q3 – Planetary Migration in Protoplanetary Discs** **[25 marks]**

**a.**

Balancing the centripetal force with the gravitational force [accept balancing accelerations]

$$M_pr_p\Omega_p^2 = \frac{GM_*M_p}{r_p^2}$$ [1] **[1]**

Cancelling $M_{\mathrm{p}}$ and rearranging gives $\Omega_p = \sqrt{\frac{GM_*}{r_p^3}}$ as required

[This was a ‘show that’, so the mark is for the algebraic route to the answer, not the final answer]

Using the equations for the hint at the end of the question

$$L = I\Omega_p = M_pr_P^2\Omega_p$$ [1] **[1]**

Substituting the expression for $\Omega_{\mathrm{p}}$ gives $L = M_p\sqrt{GM_*r_p}$ as required

[This was a ‘show that’, so the mark is for the algebraic route to the answer, not the final answer]

**b.**

We will need to integrate the surface density (mass per unit area) over the total area of the disc

$$M_{disc} = \int_{r_{in}}^{r_{out}}\Sigma\,\mathrm{d}A$$ [1]

Given $r_{\mathrm{out}} = 9r_0$ and $r_{\mathrm{in}} \ll r_0$ our lower integral limit is ≈ 0, and $\mathrm{d}A = 2\pi r\ \mathrm{d}r$ so

$$M_{disc} = \int_0^{9r_0}\Sigma_0\left(\frac{r}{r_0}\right)^{-3/2}2\pi r\ \mathrm{d}r$$ [1]

$$= \left[\Sigma_0r_0^{3/2}4\pi r^{1/2}\right]_0^{9r_0}$$ [1]

$$= 12\pi\Sigma_0r_0^2$$ [1] **[4]**

[If the first mark is not already given, it can be scored for either a correct approximation of 0 for the lower integral limit, or for converting from dA to dr. Students that do $M_{disc} = \int_0^{9r_0}\Sigma\,\mathrm{d}r = -\frac{2}{3}\Sigma_0r_0$ get a maximum of 1 mark (for the lower integral limit), since the negative total mass is non-physical]

**c.**

The final expression does not include $\delta$, so we need to find it as a function of $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ so we can combine the given expressions. Given $\Sigma \propto r^{-\alpha}$ and $P \propto r^{-\delta}$,

$\frac{P}{\Sigma T} = \text{constant} \therefore T \propto \frac{P}{\Sigma} \propto \frac{r^{-\delta}}{r^{-\alpha}} \Rightarrow T \propto r^{-\delta+\alpha}$ ① [1]

We are told it is a disc of uniform entropy (so ds = 0)

$$ds = \text{constant}\times\left(\frac{1}{\gamma-1}\frac{dT}{T} - \frac{d\Sigma}{\Sigma}\right) = 0 \therefore \frac{dT}{T} = (\gamma-1)\frac{d\Sigma}{\Sigma}$$ [1]

Using the hint given

$$\Rightarrow T \propto \Sigma^{\gamma-1}$$ [1]

But given $\Sigma \propto r^{-\alpha}$ from earlier

$\Rightarrow T \propto r^{-\alpha\gamma+\alpha}$ ② [1]

Comparing ① and ②

$$\Rightarrow \delta = \alpha\gamma$$ [1] **[5]**

Substituting this into the given expressions for $\Gamma_{\mathrm{L}}$ and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{C}}$ gives the required expression

$$\Gamma = \Gamma_L + \Gamma_C = (-3.20 + 0.86\alpha - 2.33\alpha\gamma + 5.97\times1.5 - 5.97\alpha)\Gamma_0$$

$$= (5.755 - (5.11 + 2.33\gamma)\alpha)\Gamma_0$$ [‘Show that’ so mark for route not answer]

**d.**

Using our earlier expression for L and assuming only the orbital radius changes with time

$$\Gamma = \frac{\mathrm{d}L}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(M_p\sqrt{GM_*r_p}\right) = \frac{1}{2}M_p\sqrt{GM_*}r_p^{-1/2}\frac{\mathrm{d}r_p}{\mathrm{d}t}$$ [1]

In the model of part b., $\Sigma \propto r^{-3/2}$ so by comparison with part c. $\alpha = 3/2$, and we are told $\gamma = 1.4$

Using the expression from part c. for $\Gamma$ and inputting $\Gamma_0$ with the earlier expression for $\Omega_{\mathrm{p}}$

$$\Gamma = (5.76 - (5.11 + 2.33\gamma)\alpha)\Gamma_0$$

$$= (5.76 - (5.11 + 2.33\times1.4)\times1.5)\times\left(\frac{q}{h}\right)^2\Sigma_pr_p^4\frac{GM_*}{r_p^3}$$ [1]

$$= -6.80\left(\frac{q}{h}\right)^2\Sigma_pGM_*r_p$$ [1]

Equating these two expressions for $\Gamma$ and rearranging for $\mathrm{d}r_{\mathrm{p}}/\mathrm{d}t$

$$\frac{1}{2}M_p\sqrt{GM_*}r_p^{-1/2}\frac{\mathrm{d}r_p}{\mathrm{d}t} = -6.80\left(\frac{q}{h}\right)^2\Sigma_pGM_*r_p$$

$$\therefore \frac{\mathrm{d}r_p}{\mathrm{d}t} = -13.60\left(\frac{q}{h}\right)^2\Sigma_p\frac{\sqrt{GM_*}}{M_P}r_p^{3/2}$$ [1]

However, we recognise that $\Sigma_p = \Sigma_0\left(\frac{r_p}{r_0}\right)^{-3/2}$

$$\therefore \frac{\mathrm{d}r_p}{\mathrm{d}t} = -13.60\left(\frac{q}{h}\right)^2\Sigma_0\frac{\sqrt{GM_*}}{M_P}r_0^{3/2}$$ [1]

All of the parameters on the right hand side are constant $\therefore \frac{\mathrm{d}r_p}{\mathrm{d}t} = \mathrm{constant}$, so if in time t the radius of the planet has halved, $\frac{\mathrm{d}r_p}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\frac{\frac{1}{2}r_0}{t}$ [negative since $r_{\mathrm{p}}$ is decreasing] [1]

Substituting it in and rearranging for t

$$-\frac{\frac{1}{2}r_0}{t} = -13.60\left(\frac{q}{h}\right)^2\Sigma_0\frac{\sqrt{GM_*}}{M_P}r_0^{3/2}$$

$$\therefore t = \frac{1}{27.19}\left(\frac{h}{q}\right)^2\frac{1}{\Sigma_0}\frac{M_p}{\sqrt{GM_*}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{r_0}}$$ [1]

From Kepler’s 3rd law, we can derive an expression for the initial orbital period, $\tau_0$

$$\tau_0 = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{GM_*}}r_0^{3/2}$$

$$\therefore t = \frac{1}{27.19}\left(\frac{h}{q}\right)^2\frac{M_p}{2}\frac{\tau_0}{\pi\Sigma_0r_0^2}$$ [1]

As found in part b., $M_{disc} = 12\pi\Sigma_0r_0^2$ and remembering that $q = M_p/M_*$

$$\therefore t = \frac{1}{27.19}\left(\frac{h}{q}\right)^2\frac{M_p}{2}\frac{12\tau_0}{M_{disc}} = \frac{6}{27.19}\frac{1}{h}\frac{h^3}{q}\frac{M_*}{M_{disc}}\tau_0 = \boxed{0.221t_m}$$ [1] **[9]**

[Must be in terms of the migration timescale, $t_{\mathrm{m}}$, for the final mark. The numerical factor may be left as 1/4.53 or equivalent rather than evaluated]

**e.**

Substituting the numbers into the equation we just derived

$$t = 0.221\times\frac{1}{0.05}\times\frac{0.05^3}{5\times10^{-6}}\times\frac{1}{0.01}\times10\ \text{yrs} = \boxed{110\ 000\ \text{yrs}}$$ [1] **[1]**

Since $t < 10$ Myr then $\boxed{\text{yes}}$, it is a feasible mechanism [1] **[1]**

[Award 0.5 marks for calculating $t_{\mathrm{m}}$ (= 0.5 Myr). Second mark can only be gained with a sensible comparison between their t (allowing ecf) and 10 Myr, not for a bald statement. Allow use of the more precise formula for $\Gamma$ from c. leading to 110 246 years rather than 110 327 years]

**f.**

The migration will stop when $\Gamma$ = 0, which we can use to define a critical value of $\alpha$

$$\Gamma = (5.76 - (5.11 + 2.33\gamma)\alpha_{crit})\Gamma_0 = 0$$

$$\therefore \alpha_{crit} = \frac{5.76}{5.11+2.33\gamma}$$ [1]

Since $\gamma \geq 1$ this means $0 < \alpha_{crit} < 0.774$

Far from the inner edge (as used previously in the question), $\alpha = 3/2 = 1.5$

We are told that $\Sigma$ decreases to zero at the inner edge, so the variation of $\Sigma$ as a function of increasing r must be that it starts from zero at $r_{\mathrm{inner}}$, increases smoothly to some maximum, and then decreases again following $\Sigma \propto r^{-3/2}$.

Since $\alpha = -\frac{r_p}{\Sigma_p}\left.\frac{d\Sigma}{dr}\right|_p$ then following the behaviour described above there must be a region near $r_{\mathrm{inner}}$ where $\left.\frac{d\Sigma}{dr}\right|_p$ is positive (since in that region $\Sigma$ is increasing with increasing r) and so (since $r_{\mathrm{p}}$ and $\Sigma_{\mathrm{p}}$ are also positive) $\alpha$ is negative [1]

[This mark is for any reasoning that to match the described behaviour then there must be a change in the sign of $\alpha$ as you approach $r_{\mathrm{inner}}$]

This means far from the inner edge $\alpha = 1.5 > \text{all possible } \alpha_{crit}$

and close to the inner edge $\alpha < 0 < \text{all possible } \alpha_{crit}$

so there must be a place in the disc between $r_{\mathrm{outer}}$ and $r_{\mathrm{inner}}$ where $\alpha = \alpha_{crit}$

hence $\boxed{\text{the migration does halt}}$ before the inner edge of the disc [1] **[3]**

[No mark for a bald statement without some attempt at mathematical justification]

[This is the reason planets are able to form **and** survive to be detected in mature star systems, otherwise planets would only be a feature of young systems (before spiralling into their star) and life on Earth would not have had enough time to evolve]
